questions.topic: Bending radius of a beam particle in a field

questions.stem: A transit planner sketches a proton entering a uniform magnetic field of 0.80 T at right angles with speed 3.0e6 m/s. What bending radius should be marked on the board?

options.text: About 3.9 cm, from r = mv/(qB) with qvB balancing the centripetal force.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Oscillation length of a neutrino beam
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the neutrino oscillation length scales with energy and the squared mass splitting
questions.stem: A planner's board asks why the neutrino oscillation length scales with beam energy. Explain the dependence of the length on energy and mass splitting.

answer.exemplar: The oscillation length follows L = 4 pi hbar c E / (delta m^2 c^4). Because the phase of the flavour mixing grows as delta m^2 c^4 L/(2 hbar c E), a longer path or a higher energy both slow the phase, so the distance needed for a full flavour cycle is proportional to E over delta m^2.

questions.explanation: Higher energy lengthens the path per flavour cycle, which is why long-baseline beams run at high energy. Doubling the energy doubles the length at fixed mass splitting.
questions.hint: The mixing phase sets the length.

questions.topic: Bending radius of a beam particle in a field
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the bending radius of a charged particle depends on mass, speed and field
questions.stem: The depot board asks for a written explanation of why a fast charged particle bends more sharply in a strong magnetic field.

answer.exemplar: In a uniform magnetic field the magnetic force q v B acts perpendicular to the velocity and supplies the centripetal force, so q v B = m v^2 / r. Solving gives r = m v/(q B), and because the mass and speed appear in the numerator while the field appears in the denominator, a stronger field produces a tighter curve for the same particle.

questions.explanation: A stronger field therefore tightens the curve, which is why bending magnets focus a beam as the field rises. The radius scales as one over the field.
questions.hint: Magnetic force supplies the centripetal force.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The Lorentz transform and the role of each piece
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of each term in the Lorentz transform between inertial frames
questions.stem: A planning board asks for a written explanation of the role of each term in the Lorentz transform between two inertial frames.

answer.exemplar: The Lorentz transform mixes space and time because different observers disagree about simultaneity. For a frame moving at speed v along the x axis, the time coordinate combines the original time with the distance along the motion, x' = gamma (x - v t) and t' = gamma (t - v x / c^2), with gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2). The mixing terms are what allow one frame to be consistent with all observers.

questions.explanation: The gamma factor keeps the light cone invariant, so every observer still measures the same speed of light. That consistency is the point of the transform.
questions.hint: Simultaneity is frame dependent.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Fastest electron from a weak decay
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the electron spectrum in a beta decay has a definite endpoint
questions.stem: A board asks for a written account of why the fastest electron from a weak decay has a definite endpoint energy rather than a continuum of energies.

answer.exemplar: In a weak decay such as neutron beta decay the available energy is shared between the electron, an antineutrino and the recoiling parent, so the electron alone receives a range of energies. The extreme case is the endpoint, where the neutrino takes essentially no energy and the electron carries the whole available release minus the small parent recoil, which fixes the maximum kinetic energy at about 0.782 MeV for a free neutron.

questions.explanation: The three-body sharing of energy means the electron can take any value from near zero up to the endpoint, where the neutrino carries nothing. The endpoint is slightly below the full mass release.
questions.hint: Endpoint means the neutrino takes no energy.

questions.topic: Bending radius of a beam particle in a field
questions.learningObjective: Explain why bending magnets on a beam line alternate in polarity
questions.stem: A written explanation is requested on the board for why the bending magnets on a beam line are arranged in alternating polarity.

answer.exemplar: Alternating polarity lets the beam alternate between bending up and bending down, so the net deflection over a cell is close to zero while the path still curves. Each magnet acts as a lens for the beam, focusing in one transverse plane and defocusing in the other, and the alternating pattern lets the cell as a whole keep the beam tightly focused while it advances down the line.

questions.explanation: The sequence keeps the beam small without turning the whole line, and each cell focuses in one plane while defocusing in the other.
questions.hint: Focusing in one plane, defocusing in the other.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The Lorentz transform and the role of each piece
questions.learningObjective: Explain why absolute uniform motion cannot be detected by any internal experiment
questions.stem: On the question of absolute motion, a board asks for a written explanation of why no observer can detect uniform motion through a vacuum.

answer.exemplar: The laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, so the equations that describe them must be invariant under the change from one frame to another. The Lorentz transform is the unique way to change between inertial frames while preserving the speed of light and the form of Maxwell's equations, so no experiment performed entirely inside a frame can reveal that frame's uniform velocity relative to anything else.

questions.explanation: A uniform velocity can only be detected relative to something else, never by an internal experiment carried out inside one frame.
questions.hint: The laws of physics are frame independent.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Fastest electron from a weak decay
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a magnetic spectrometer separates particles of different momentum
questions.stem: On the topic of a magnetic spectrometer, a board asks for a written account of how particles of different momentum in a decay are separated.

answer.exemplar: A momentum spectrometer works by bending the particles in a known magnetic field and measuring the curvature of the path. Since the radius of curvature is proportional to momentum for a given charge and field, particles with different momenta follow different arcs, and placing a detector in the focal plane of the magnet converts the curvature difference into a position difference that identifies the momentum of each particle.

questions.explanation: The trap is to think the field changes the speed; it only changes the direction, and the momentum sets the radius.
questions.hint: Curvature of the path encodes the momentum.

questions.stem: A tuning request on the board asks for a written explanation of how a neutrino beam is prepared so that its flavour content is known before the far detector.

answer.exemplar: A beam of neutral particles does not reveal its flavour by itself, so the accelerator complex injects a known neutrino flavour and lets the beam travel a short distance where the oscillation phase is still small, so the outgoing beam keeps essentially its original flavour. A detector placed at that point measures the interaction rate of that known flavour, and the ratio of near and far detector rates then gives the probability of flavour change along the long baseline.

questions.explanation: The far detector sees a reduced rate for that flavour, and the ratio of the two rates gives the oscillation probability.
questions.hint: Compare the near and far detectors.

questions.stem: On the charge dependence, a board asks for a written explanation of how the bending radius of a beam particle changes with the charge and the field.

answer.exemplar: The bending radius follows from r = p/(q B) for motion perpendicular to the field, so the radius is inversely proportional to the field strength and inversely proportional to the charge.
